brief: Epictetus' dichotomy of control (Enchiridion 1 and 5), the Stoic archer (Cicero, De Finibus III), James Stockdale, links to CBT (Ellis, Beck).
Hedonic adaptation: Brickman & Campbell 1971, lottery study 1978, Diener/Lucas/Scollon 2006 revision, Seneca Letter 2, Epicurus Vatican Saying 35, gratitude practice.

Memento mori in Stoicism: Marcus Aurelius (Meditations II.11, IV.17), Seneca 'On the Shortness of Life', how awareness of death clarifies priorities; terror management theory as a modern psychological counterpart (Greenberg, Pyszczynski, Solomon).

The spotlight effect: Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky (2000) Barry Manilow T-shirt study; the illusion of transparency; why others notice us far less than we think; link to Stoic indifference to reputation.

Amor fati: Nietzsche (The Gay Science §276, Ecce Homo), Marcus Aurelius on accepting what happens (Meditations IV.23, VIII.47 style), Epictetus Enchiridion 8 ('wish things to happen as they do'); acceptance vs resignation.

Cognitive dissonance: Leon Festinger (1957), 'When Prophecy Fails' (1956) doomsday group study, Festinger & Carlsmith 1959 one-dollar/twenty-dollar experiment; Aesop's fox and the grapes; how to notice self-justification.
Albert Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus (1942): the absurd, rejecting escape, revolt, freedom, passion; 'One must imagine Sisyphus happy'; meaning in repetitive everyday life.
Negativity bias: Baumeister et al. (2001) 'Bad is stronger than good', Rozin & Royzman (2001), evolutionary explanation; loss aversion (Kahneman & Tversky); practical ways to rebalance attention.
Plato's allegory of the cave (Republic, Book VII): shadows, the turning around, the painful ascent, returning to the cave; modern parallels with information bubbles and comfortable illusions.
Flow: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (Flow, 1990), challenge-skill balance, experience sampling method; deep focus vs distraction; Aristotle's idea that happiness lies in activity.
Seneca, De Brevitate Vitae: 'Life is long if you know how to use it'; how people guard money but squander time; busyness (occupati); practical reflections on attention and time.
Impostor phenomenon: Pauline Clance & Suzanne Imes (1978), not a clinical diagnosis, prevalence across groups, link to perfectionism; Socratic humility as a healthier counterpart.
'Know thyself' (Delphi), Socrates' 'the unexamined life is not worth living' (Plato, Apology 38a), Socratic ignorance; modern research on the limits of introspection (Nisbett & Wilson 1977).
Peak-end rule and duration neglect: Kahneman et al. cold-water study (1993), Redelmeier & Kahneman colonoscopy study (1996); experiencing self vs remembering self; designing endings.

Pascal, Pensées: 'all of humanity's problems stem from man's inability to sit quietly in a room alone'; diversion (divertissement); Wilson et al. (2014) study where people preferred mild electric shocks to sitting alone with their thoughts.
Sunk cost fallacy: Arkes & Blumer (1985) theater ticket study, escalation of commitment (Staw), letting go; Stoic perspective that the past is not in our control.
Wu wei in Daoism: Laozi's Daodejing (water imagery, chapter 8 and 78), Zhuangzi's Cook Ding story; effortless action vs passivity; connection to flow.

Self-compassion: Kristin Neff's three components (self-kindness, common humanity, mindfulness), difference from self-esteem and self-pity; Seneca's daily self-examination (On Anger III.36) done gently.
Heraclitus and change: 'you cannot step into the same river twice' (as reported by Plato, Cratylus 402a), panta rhei, unity of opposites; impermanence and the changing self.
Confirmation bias: Peter Wason's 2-4-6 task (1960), selective exposure, Francis Bacon's Novum Organum (1620) on the human understanding; practical habits of seeking disconfirmation.

Viktor Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning (1946): the last of human freedoms, logotherapy, meaning through work, love and suffering; Nietzsche's 'he who has a why to live can bear almost any how' as Frankl quotes it.
Fundamental attribution error: Jones & Harris (1967) Castro essay study, Ross (1977) naming it; Marcus Aurelius on others' wrongdoing (Meditations II.1); charitable interpretation.
Epicurus on death: 'Death is nothing to us' (Letter to Menoeceus, Principal Doctrines 2), the tetrapharmakos (four-part cure), Lucretius' symmetry argument (De Rerum Natura III).
Learned helplessness: Seligman & Maier (1967) and Maier & Seligman's 2016 revision (passivity is default, control is learned); explanatory style; learned optimism. Avoid clinical advice.
Aristotle's doctrine of the mean (Nicomachean Ethics II): courage between cowardice and rashness, virtue as habit ('we become just by doing just acts'), eudaimonia.

Bystander effect: Darley & Latané (1968) seizure and smoke-filled room studies; the Kitty Genovese story and how the original reporting exaggerated it; Philpot et al. (2020) CCTV study showing intervention is common.

Diogenes of Sinope: living in a jar (pithos), the lamp in daylight, Alexander the Great anecdote ('stand out of my sunlight'), Cynic freedom from convention; anecdotes come from Diogenes Laertius and should be framed as tradition.
Unfinished tasks: Bluma Zeigarnik (1927) and the mixed replication record; Masicampo & Baumeister (2011) showing that making a plan reduces intrusive thoughts about unfinished goals.
Kierkegaard, The Concept of Anxiety (1844): 'anxiety is the dizziness of freedom', possibility and choice, the leap; anxiety as a sign of freedom rather than only a problem.
Choice overload: Iyengar & Lepper (2000) jam study, Barry Schwartz's maximizers vs satisficers, Scheibehenne et al. (2010) meta-analysis showing mixed effects; when fewer options help.
Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy (c. 524), written in prison awaiting execution: Lady Philosophy, the wheel of Fortune, true vs false goods.

Delay of gratification: Walter Mischel's marshmallow studies (Stanford, late 1960s–70s), follow-ups, Watts, Duncan & Quan (2018) conceptual replication showing smaller effects once family background is controlled; Kidd et al. (2013) on reliability of the environment.
Marcus Aurelius' morning reflections: Meditations II.1 (preparing for difficult people), V.1 (getting out of bed), writing to himself not for publication; the inner citadel (Pierre Hadot).

Rumination vs reflection: Susan Nolen-Hoeksema's research on rumination, brooding vs reflective pondering (Treynor et al. 2003), distanced self-talk (Kross et al. 2014). Educational, not clinical advice.
Simone Weil on attention: 'Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity' (letter to Joë Bousquet, 1942), Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies; attention in a distracted age.
Locus of control: Julian Rotter (1966), internal vs external, links to well-being and agency; nuance that realistic appraisal matters; parallel with Epictetus.
Montaigne's Essays: 'Que sais-je?', 'To philosophize is to learn to die', his tower library, honesty about himself, friendship with La Boétie ('because it was he, because it was I').
Mere exposure effect: Robert Zajonc (1968), familiarity breeds liking, implications for taste, relationships and advertising; noticing why we like what we like.
Spinoza's Ethics (1677) on the emotions: understanding an emotion lessens its power (Part V, Prop. 3), freedom as understanding necessity, joy and sadness as changes in power.

How habits work: Wendy Wood's research (about 43% of daily actions are habitual, Wood, Quinn & Kashy 2002), Lally et al. (2010) habit formation taking a median of 66 days with wide variation; Aristotle on virtue as habit.
